name: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate

angle.text: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate is an oil-soluble vitamin C ester used in serums for brightening and anti-aging as a gentler alternative to L-ascorbic acid. Human data come from small product-level studies.

summary: An oil-soluble vitamin C ester for serums; human data come from small, product-level studies.
note: Trials test multi-ingredient products and are often company-linked.
currentQuick:
Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate is a fat-soluble form of vitamin C used in brightening and anti-ageing serums, positioned as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid.
Studies are small and test whole regimens, so its own effect is not isolated.
How it works: As an ascorbate ester it is used as an antioxidant and pigment-modulating vitamin C source; lab work shows it can degrade under oxidative stress unless stabilised.
Risks and caveats: Trials of products containing it report generally good tolerance; no specific serious safety signals were found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate (THD ascorbate, THDA) is an oil-soluble ester derivative of vitamin C used in serums and moisturisers marketed for brightening and anti-ageing. It is used as an alternative to L-ascorbic acid, which is described as unstable and sometimes irritating at high concentrations .
Human data on THDA specifically are limited to small, mostly manufacturer-associated studies of multi-ingredient products. A 2021 laboratory study reported that it degrades rapidly under oxidative stress but can be stabilised by acetyl zingerone , and a 2024 randomized double-blind study compared THDA with and without acetyl zingerone on facial photoaging .

name: Ethyl ascorbic acid

chain: Inhibits tyrosinase as vitamin C form
angle.text: Ethyl ascorbic acid is a vitamin C derivative sold for brightening and anti-aging, used by people chasing an even, radiant complexion. It is supported by lab studies, with no controlled human trials found.

summary: A vitamin C ether sold for brightening; supported by lab studies, with no controlled human trials found.
note: At least one reported case of allergic contact dermatitis.
currentQuick:
Ethyl ascorbic acid is a modified vitamin C used in brightening serums.
Published work is mostly on cells and animal skin; no controlled human trials were found.
How it works: Lab studies report it inhibits tyrosinase and melanin production in cultured cells and has antioxidant effects in UV-exposed keratinocytes.
Risks and caveats: A case report documented allergic contact dermatitis from cosmetics containing it. Systematic safety data are limited.
deepLead:
3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid (ethyl ascorbic acid, EAC) is an ether derivative of vitamin C used in brightening and anti-ageing skincare. It is described as a tyrosinase inhibitor and is widely used in formulations, although the mechanisms behind its effects have been described as poorly understood .
Evidence for it in people is sparse. The bulk of published work consists of cell and animal-skin studies, formulation and analysis papers, and at least one case report of allergic contact dermatitis .

name: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate

chain: Converts to vitamin C in skin
angle.text: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate is a stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative used in cosmetics mainly as an antioxidant, and people use it for brighter skin and acne marks. Formulation data are plentiful; human appearance outcomes are sparse.

summary: A stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative; formulation data are plentiful, human appearance outcomes are sparse.
note: Registered acne and photoaging trials exist but outcomes were not located.
currentQuick:
Sodium ascorbyl phosphate is a stabilised, water-soluble form of vitamin C used as a cosmetic antioxidant.
Most published work covers formulation and stability; human trials of its looks effects are few.
How it works: It functions primarily as an antioxidant in cosmetic formulations, per the Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment.
Risks and caveats: A cosmetic safety assessment covers SAP alongside other vitamin C compounds; no specific harms were found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Sodium ascorbyl phosphate (SAP) is a water-soluble, phosphate-ester derivative of vitamin C used in cosmetics, mainly as an antioxidant. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review's safety assessment of ascorbic acid and its salts and esters, including SAP, describes them as functioning primarily as antioxidants in cosmetic formulations .
SAP is promoted as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid. Laboratory studies have examined its stability in microemulsions and in formulations containing lipoic acid and vitamins A and E . Human evidence includes a registered trial of a 5% SAP lotion for acne and trials of topical antioxidant regimens for photoaging .

name: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate

chain: Converts to vitamin C in skin
angle.text: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a stable vitamin C pro-drug found in brightening serums, used for even tone and a fresher look. It is common in products but thin on direct human trials.

summary: A stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative in brightening serums; common in products, thin on direct human trials.
note: Human data specific to MAP are sparse; most vitamin C evidence concerns L-ascorbic acid.
currentQuick:
Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a vitamin C derivative used in cosmetic serums and creams. It is promoted as being more stable than pure ascorbic acid.
Published evidence for its appearance effects is limited; one small study reported improved skin hydration, and reviews say clinical data on topical vitamin C are limited overall.
How it works: It is described as a pro-drug that is converted to ascorbic acid in skin. Laboratory studies show it is more stable than ascorbic acid in formulations, while penetration into skin is the main challenge discussed in the literature.
Risks and caveats: A cosmetic safety assessment covering MAP was published in 2005. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold without prescription; product labels advise external use and avoiding the eyes.
deepLead:
Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate (MAP) is a water-soluble derivative of vitamin C used as an ingredient in skincare products, where it is marketed as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid. It is described in the literature as a pro-drug of vitamin C, meaning it is meant to be converted to ascorbic acid after reaching the skin. 
Laboratory work has found that ascorbic acid and its derivatives are more stable as ascorbyl esters than as the free acid in solution and in topical formulations.  A cosmetic ingredient safety review covering ascorbic acid and several of its salts and phosphate esters, including MAP, was published in the International Journal of Toxicology in 2005. 
Evidence for MAP specifically on appearance outcomes is limited. One small formulation study reported improved skin hydration with a MAP product, while a broader review of topical vitamin C notes that clinical studies of topical formulations are limited and that stability and penetration are the main challenges.

name: Superoxide dismutase

angle.text: Superoxide dismutase is an antioxidant enzyme added to anti-aging products on the idea that limiting oxidative stress keeps skin looking younger. It is biologically central, but its cosmetic effect on appearance is essentially unstudied.

summary: An antioxidant enzyme added to anti-aging products; biologically central, but cosmetic evidence is essentially unstudied.
note: Registered trials concern radiation skin injury and oral supplements, not cosmetic anti-aging.
currentQuick:
Superoxide dismutase is a naturally occurring enzyme family that neutralizes the superoxide radical. It is added to some topical products and oral supplements marketed for antioxidant skin protection.
No published trial of topical SOD for cosmetic anti-aging was found; registered human trials concern mostly radiation skin injury and oral supplements.
How it works: SOD converts superoxide into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. Humans have cytosolic (SOD1), mitochondrial (SOD2) and extracellular (SOD3) forms.
Risks and caveats: No cosmetic-specific safety data were found. Wikipedia notes that bovine-derived SOD drugs were withdrawn in several European countries over prion concerns.
deepLead:
Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is a family of metalloenzymes that convert the superoxide radical into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide and is regarded as a first line of antioxidant defense in most oxygen-using organisms.  The enzymatic activity was identified in 1969 by James McCord and Irwin Fridovich in a copper protein from red blood cells. 
In skincare, SOD is added to products marketed as antioxidant or anti-photoaging. No published trial of topical SOD for cosmetic anti-aging was found. Registered human trials of SOD have mostly concerned radiation-related skin injury and oral supplements.

name: Ubiquinone topical

angle.text: Topical coenzyme Q10 is included in anti-aging creams, with reports of reduced photoaging and wrinkle depth. Skin penetration is a recognised hurdle, and direct wrinkle trials are scarce.

summary: The mitochondrial antioxidant in many anti-aging creams; skin penetration is a recognized hurdle and direct wrinkle trials are scarce.
note: Topical trials found are in oral or eye conditions, not facial aging.
currentQuick:
Coenzyme Q10 is a compound the body makes in mitochondria, and it is added to anti-aging creams for antioxidant effects. One formulation paper says cosmetic CoQ10 has been reported to reduce photoaging, but that skin bioavailability is poor.
Human trials of topical CoQ10 identified here concern oral and eye conditions rather than wrinkles.
How it works: It carries electrons in the mitochondrial chain and its reduced form acts as an antioxidant. Delivery systems such as liposomes have been studied to improve skin uptake.
Risks and caveats: Oral CoQ10 is described as generally well tolerated. Topical-specific safety data were not found, and it is sold as a cosmetic or supplement rather than an approved anti-aging drug.
deepLead:
Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, ubiquinone) is a fat-soluble, quinone compound found in cell membranes and involved in mitochondrial electron transport, and it also acts as an antioxidant.  It is included in some anti-aging creams, and the literature describes cosmetically applied CoQ10 as having been reported to reduce photoaging and wrinkle depth, while noting that its bioavailability through skin is poor. 
Formulation research has therefore focused on delivery systems such as liposomes.  Most controlled human trials of topical CoQ10 identified in the sources reviewed are in oral or eye conditions rather than facial aging.

name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a collagen-signal peptide that is one half of Matrixyl 3000, used in serums for wrinkles and firmness. Evidence is mostly lab and permeation data.

summary: The collagen-signal peptide half of Matrixyl 3000; widely used, with mostly lab and permeation data behind it.
note: Origin story comes largely from an AI-generated reference; human efficacy trials are sparse.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a lab-made peptide (glycine-histidine-lysine plus a fatty acid) used in anti-wrinkle creams and serums. It is one of the two peptides in Matrixyl 3000.
Recent published work is mostly laboratory, permeation and computational studies; no dedicated wrinkle trial was found.
How it works: It is described as a signal peptide that prompts skin fibroblasts to make collagen and matrix. The fatty acid chain is meant to help it cross the skin barrier, though one study found the peptides stayed in the outer layer.
Risks and caveats: Product labels advise external use only, avoiding eyes, and stopping if irritation occurs. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 (Pal-GHK) is a synthetic lipopeptide made of the amino acids glycine, histidine and lysine joined to palmitic acid, used in cosmetic skincare.  It is marketed as a collagen-stimulating signal peptide and is one of the two peptides in the branded blend Matrixyl 3000. 
Grokipedia attributes its development to the French ingredient company Sederma around 2000, building on the GHK peptide reported in human plasma in 1973 (this account is from an AI-generated source).  Published evidence for wrinkle reduction in people is limited in the sources reviewed; recent papers are laboratory or permeation studies.

name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7

angle.text: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Rigin) is an anti-inflammatory signal peptide, the second peptide in Matrixyl 3000, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products. Little isolated human data exist.

summary: The anti-inflammatory peptide half of Matrixyl 3000; present in many serums, with little isolated human data.
note: Mechanism claims come largely from lab data and an AI-generated reference.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a lab-made peptide with a fatty acid tail, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products. It is paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1 in Matrixyl 3000.
Its effects in people have mostly been studied inside multi-ingredient products, not on its own.
How it works: In lab models it is reported to reduce inflammatory IL-6 release and to support skin matrix proteins.
Risks and caveats: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient; labels advise external use only and avoiding the eyes. No ingredient-specific safety data were found.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Pal-GQPR, sold as Rigin) is a synthetic peptide of glycine, glutamine, proline and arginine attached to palmitic acid and used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin cosmetics.  It is described as an anti-inflammatory signal peptide and is the second peptide in Matrixyl 3000. 
Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports it decreases IL-6 secretion in lab models.  Peptides in general are widely used in sensitive-skin products, according to an analysis of 88 facial cosmetics.  Published human efficacy data specific to this peptide are limited.

name: Matrixyl 3000

angle.text: Matrixyl 3000 is Sederma's two-peptide blend found in many anti-wrinkle serums, promoted for smoother, firmer skin. There is little independent human data on the blend itself.

summary: Sederma's two-peptide anti-wrinkle blend; ubiquitous in serums, little independent human data on the blend itself.
note: Sources for this entry are thin.
currentQuick:
Matrixyl 3000 is a branded pairing of two lab-made peptides used in anti-wrinkle serums.
Independent published human data on the blend are limited.
How it works: Its peptides are proposed to signal skin cells to repair matrix and reduce inflammation; one study found they stay in the skin surface layers.
Risks and caveats: A cosmetic ingredient; no blend-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Matrixyl 3000 is a branded peptide complex made by Sederma that combines palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, and is used in anti-wrinkle serums.  Its predecessor, Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4), was launched by Sederma in 2000. 
Published evidence on the blend itself is limited: a 2026 permeation study reported that both peptides were detected in layers of the stratum corneum of three volunteers but appeared to remain between cells.

name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 (Syn-Coll) is a collagen-signalling peptide in anti-wrinkle creams, serums and microneedle patches, promoted for firmness. Evidence is small-scale and from multi-ingredient products.

summary: A collagen-signalling cosmetic peptide (Syn-Coll) with only multi-ingredient, small-scale evidence behind it.
note: Evidence comes from multi-ingredient products; no isolated placebo-controlled trial found.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 is a lab-made peptide attached to a fatty acid, added to anti-ageing creams and serums. It is marketed as telling skin cells to produce more collagen.
Published evidence is thin: studies have tested it mixed with other ingredients, and no standalone placebo-controlled human trial was found.
How it works: Suppliers say it acts as a signal peptide that stimulates collagen synthesis via a TGF-beta-related pathway; the fatty chain is intended to help it cross the outer skin layer. This is mainly manufacturer description.
Risks and caveats: No specific safety problems are documented in the sources found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-5, sold under the trade name Syn-Coll, is a synthetic lipopeptide used as an ingredient in anti-wrinkle and skin-firming cosmetics. It is marketed as a "signal peptide" intended to prompt skin cells to make more collagen, and it appears in creams, serums and microneedle patches.
Published material on the ingredient is sparse. A clinical study of hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several bioactive peptides evaluated tolerability and skin effects of a multi-peptide product , and laboratory work has used it as a component of collagen nanoparticle formulations . No published trial appears to isolate palmitoyl tripeptide-5 as a single active against placebo.

name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8

angle.text: Skincare users with sensitive or reddish skin look to this peptide (sold as Neutrazen) to calm irritation and reduce visible redness for a more even-looking face. It is promoted for this in cosmetics; standalone human data for that use are essentially absent.

summary: A soothing anti-redness cosmetic peptide (Neutrazen) with essentially no standalone human data.
note: Only multi-ingredient or lab data found.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-8 is a lab-made peptide used in products for sensitive, red or irritated skin. It is marketed under the name Neutrazen.
No human trial of the peptide on its own was found; the existing research is laboratory work or tests of blended formulas.
How it works: Suppliers describe it as dampening inflammatory signalling in skin. Laboratory work has also used it as a targeting molecule for the melanocortin 1 receptor in liposome delivery.
Risks and caveats: Product labels advise a patch test and stopping use if irritation occurs. No specific adverse-effect literature was found.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-8, marketed as Neutrazen, is a synthetic lipopeptide used in cosmetics for sensitive or redness-prone skin. It is promoted as calming irritation-related redness and discomfort.
It has been identified among the peptides used in facial products for sensitive skin . Published evidence on its own effects is limited to formulation and laboratory work, often in multi-ingredient products .

name: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12

angle.text: Anti-aging cream users choose this elastin-derived peptide (Biopeptide EL) hoping for firmer, more elastic skin and a smoother look. The evidence for that use sits at lab level, and no clinical trials were found.

summary: An elastin-fragment cosmetic peptide (Biopeptide EL) with lab-level evidence and no clinical trials found.
note: No human trials found.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a lab-made peptide based on an elastin sequence, added to anti-ageing creams for elasticity.
Only early laboratory research exists; no clinical trial was found.
How it works: It is described as a self-assembling peptide that interacts with skin components and may alter skin mechanics, based on a 2025 imaging study.
Risks and caveats: No ingredient-specific harms were found; safety frameworks for cosmetic peptides are still evolving.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12, sold as Biopeptide EL, is a synthetic fatty-acid-linked peptide derived from a repeating elastin sequence and used in anti-ageing creams. It is marketed as supporting skin elasticity.
A 2025 laboratory study using label-free imaging techniques examined its short-term effects on human skin composition and mechanics, describing it as a self-assembling peptide with potential skincare benefits . No clinical trial results were found.

name: Palmitoyl oligopeptide

angle.text: Palmitoyl oligopeptide is a generic label on anti-aging creams, where it is described as a collagen-promoting signal ingredient meant to give firmer, smoother-looking skin. The collagen claim appears in patent literature; no clinical trial of the ingredient itself was found.

summary: A generic palmitoylated peptide label in anti-ageing creams, with no clinical trial of its own.
note: Generic term; specific peptides differ.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl oligopeptide is an ingredient-list term for short peptides attached to a fatty acid, used in anti-ageing creams.
No dedicated clinical trial was found.
How it works: Formulators describe such peptides as promoting collagen synthesis; the fatty chain is intended to aid skin penetration.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms were found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl oligopeptide is a generic cosmetic-ingredient name for short peptides linked to palmitic acid, used in anti-ageing creams as collagen-promoting "signal" ingredients. Patent literature lists fatty-acid-grafted peptides, specifically C16 palmitoyl oligopeptides, among agents said to promote collagen synthesis .
Published evidence specific to the ingredient is limited. A 2015 methods study used imaging and histology to evaluate extracellular matrix and the epidermal-dermal junction, and examined effects of age and peptide applications .

name: Manganese tripeptide-1

angle.text: Users of facial serums reach for this manganese analogue of GHK to address sun damage and dark spots and even out skin tone. One small study sits behind the use, so the evidence for the brightening effect is limited.

summary: A manganese-bound GHK-style peptide in serums for sun damage and dark spots, with one small study behind it.
note: Human evidence is one small facial study of a finished serum.
currentQuick:
Manganese tripeptide-1 is a cosmetic peptide complex used in facial serums for photodamaged skin. It is described as a manganese counterpart of the copper peptide GHK.
A single 12-week facial study reported improvement in photodamage signs, especially pigmentation, as judged by participants and a blinded investigator.
How it works: The published study does not establish a mechanism; the ingredient is presented as an analogue of GHK-type peptides.
Risks and caveats: The one study reported good tolerability with no significant inflammation. Long-term and comparative safety data have not been published in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Manganese tripeptide-1 is a cosmetic ingredient consisting of a manganese complex of a tripeptide, described as the manganese analogue of the copper-binding peptide GHK. It is used in facial serums marketed for photodamaged skin, including uneven pigmentation.
The published human evidence is limited to a single open-label-style facial study in which participants used a serum containing the complex twice daily for up to 12 weeks. The investigators reported improvement in several photodamage signs, most notably hyperpigmentation, and good tolerability . Independent controlled trials have not been identified.

name: Tripeptide-3

angle.text: Oily-skin users see tripeptide-3 in products marketed for oil control, aiming for a less shiny, more matte face. Published evidence under this name is thin, limited to one small 2024 delivery study.

summary: A cosmetic peptide marketed for oil control, with one small 2024 delivery study as its published evidence.
note: Little published under this name.
currentQuick:
Tripeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide listed in peptide ingredient guides. The one study found describes nanoemulsions carrying it to reduce facial oil.
Volunteers in that study showed lower sebum and higher moisture over 28 days.
How it works: The study focused on how to get the hydrophilic peptide into skin; the mechanism by which it affects sebum is not described in the abstract.
Risks and caveats: The study included an irritation assessment, but details are limited. No wider safety literature was found.
deepLead:
Tripeptide-3 is an INCI name for a short synthetic peptide used in cosmetics, including products aimed at reducing facial oiliness. Little is published about it under this name.
A 2024 pharmaceutics study developed nanoemulsions to deliver Tripeptide-3 to the skin and reported that, in healthy volunteers over 28 days, the formulation decreased sebum production and increased skin moisture .

name: Tripeptide-10 citrulline

angle.text: Anti-aging skincare users seek this peptide (Decorinyl) for tidier collagen fibres and firmer, smoother skin. Support comes from in vitro data and one 24-person study.

summary: A decorin-mimicking peptide meant to tidy collagen fibres, backed by in vitro data and one 24-person study.
note: Clinical data are small and tested mostly in combination.
currentQuick:
Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a cosmetic peptide modeled on decorin, a molecule that organizes collagen fibres. It is sold as Decorinyl in anti-wrinkle products.
Lab tests showed more uniform collagen fibres, and a small randomized study reported skin-surface changes.
How it works: It is designed to bind collagen like decorin, regulating fibril diameter and cohesion in vitro.
Risks and caveats: The published abstracts do not report adverse effects; safety data beyond these studies were not found.
deepLead:
Tripeptide-10 citrulline (marketed as Decorinyl) is a synthetic peptide designed to mimic the collagen-binding behavior of decorin, a proteoglycan that regulates collagen fibre assembly. It is used in anti-aging cosmetics.
In vitro work reported that it made collagen fibres thinner and more uniform , and a 24-person randomized study of its combination with acetyl hexapeptide-3 reported measurable changes in skin microtopography and transepidermal water loss .

name: Acetyl hexapeptide-3

angle.text: Known as Argireline, this peptide is promoted as a topical alternative to Botox for softening expression lines around the eyes and forehead. It has been studied in humans for wrinkle depth, with modest and inconsistent results.

summary: The older name for Argireline, the topical 'Botox-alternative' peptide with modest, inconsistent evidence.
note: Poor skin penetration; no direct comparison with botulinum toxin.
currentQuick:
Acetyl hexapeptide-3 is the older name of Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-8), a cosmetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for expression lines.
Studies suggest it may improve the look of wrinkles, but results are inconsistent and hard to compare.
How it works: It copies a fragment of SNAP-25 and is proposed to interfere with the SNARE complex that triggers muscle-activating neurotransmitter release. Its poor skin absorption is an active research topic.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse effects in the cited studies were minimal. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold over the counter.
deepLead:
Acetyl hexapeptide-3 is the earlier name for the cosmetic peptide now listed under the INCI name acetyl hexapeptide-8 and sold as Argireline. It is a six-amino-acid fragment (Ac-Glu-Glu-Met-Gln-Arg-Arg-NH2) of SNAP-25, a protein involved in neurotransmitter release . Wikipedia notes that the "-3" name is considered incorrect for this peptide .
It is marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for expression lines. It is proposed to interfere with SNARE complex formation and so dampen muscle contraction . Wikipedia states that no dedicated double-blind trials of its wrinkle efficacy were available and that results across studies are inconsistent . Its large, hydrophilic structure limits skin penetration, prompting microneedle and iontophoresis research .

name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-15

angle.text: Used in products for sensitive or reactive skin (sold as Skinasensyl), it is promoted as reducing nerve-driven irritation so skin looks calmer. Evidence is supplier data only; no independent studies were found.

summary: A sensitive-skin soothing peptide with supplier data only; no independent studies found.
note: Supporting data is supplier-reported; a 2021 review found no peer-reviewed studies.
currentQuick:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-15 is a cosmetic peptide marketed under the name Skinasensyl for easily irritated skin. It is a minor ingredient, found in about 2 of 88 sensitive-skin products surveyed.
Its supporting evidence is a supplier cell study and a 20-person capsaicin test; a 2021 review found no peer-reviewed publications on it.
How it works: It is described as derived from endomorphin-2 and as acting on mu-opioid receptors to dampen sensory nerve signalling, indirectly reducing TRPV1 responses and CGRP release.
Risks and caveats: No specific adverse events are reported; the review cites supplier safety data. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a medicine.
deepLead:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-15, sold by its supplier under the trade name Skinasensyl, is a synthetic peptide used in cosmetics aimed at sensitive or reactive skin. A 2021 review describes it as derived from endomorphin-2, a mu-opioid receptor agonist, and proposes that it raises the excitability threshold of skin sensory nerves in an endorphin-like way .
Supplier-reported work cited in that review includes an in vitro finding that the peptide reduced release of the neuropeptide CGRP from sensory neurons, an effect weakened by the opioid blocker naloxone, and a split-face study in 20 people reporting a higher capsaicin discomfort threshold after four days of use . The same review states that no studies of the compound were found in the scientific literature, only a patent and supplier documents .
It appears in a small share of sensitive-skin products: about 2.3 percent of 88 facial cosmetics analysed in the review . It is not a drug and has no approved medical use.

name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2

angle.text: Marketed in skin-firming and anti-aging products (such as Thymulen 4), it is claimed to support epidermal regeneration for firmer skin. Evidence consists of cell-culture data and one combination-lotion hair study, not a skin-firmness trial.

summary: A thymopoietin-mimic cosmetic peptide with cell-culture data and one combination-lotion hair study.
note: No trial of the peptide alone; the hair study used a multi-ingredient lotion.
currentQuick:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a short cosmetic peptide marketed for firmness and skin regeneration, and also appears in some hair lotions.
Research is thin: a keratinocyte cell study and a randomized study of a lotion that combined it with creatine and B vitamins.
How it works: Suppliers say it mimics thymopoietin and prompts keratinocytes to release GM-CSF, activating skin Langerhans cells. In cultured cells it raised stiffness and COL17A1 expression.
Risks and caveats: No safety data were found beyond its status as a cosmetic ingredient; the supporting claims are largely manufacturer-reported.
deepLead:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide (acetyl-Lys-Asp-Val-Tyr) used in anti-aging and skin-firming cosmetics, sold by suppliers under names such as Thymulen 4 . It is described as mimicking thymopoietin, a thymus hormone, and is claimed to counter the age-related decline of thymic factors and to support skin immune defences and epidermal regeneration .
Published research is limited. A 2018 cell study found that the peptide changed the stiffness and gene expression of cultured keratinocytes , and a 2021 randomized study tested a hair lotion that combined it with creatine and B vitamins . No trial has tested the peptide alone on facial wrinkles or firmness.

name: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester

angle.text: Sensitive-skin users choose this soothing peptide (Calmosensine) to reduce stinging and redness for a calmer complexion. Supplier data support it, while one head-to-head trial found no significant stinging benefit.

summary: A soothing peptide for sensitive skin with supplier data and one head-to-head trial showing no significant stinging benefit.
note: A 2016 capsaicin test found no significant effect for a product containing it.
currentQuick:
Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester is a peptide derivative sold as Calmosensine for sensitive, stinging-prone skin, and appears in some dermatology-brand soothing creams.
Supplier tests report comfort benefits, while a 31-woman capsaicin test of a finished product found no significant effect versus a comparator cream.
How it works: It is proposed to boost POMC expression, raising alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin, which lowers CGRP release and so reduces nerve-driven stinging and inflammation.
Risks and caveats: No specific adverse events are reported in the review; supplier safety data and CIR assessments are cited. It is a cosmetic ingredient.
deepLead:
Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, marketed as Calmosensine (also written Neurosensine), is a synthetic peptide derivative used in soothing skincare for sensitive skin. A 2021 review describes it as derived from the dipeptide Tyr-Arg and proposes that it increases expression of the POMC gene, raising levels of MSH, ACTH and beta-endorphin, which in turn is thought to lower release of CGRP and so reduce stinging indirectly .
Supplier-reported studies describe reduced heat perception and improved comfort, but the one independent-style comparison in the available sources literature, a 2016 split-face capsaicin test in 31 women, found no significant effect of a product containing it compared with a product containing 4-t-butylcyclohexanol, and the review notes that the product bases differed . It appeared in about 5.7 percent of 88 sensitive-skin products surveyed .
